items.title: [Bug]: send_message tool and cron delivery skip message chunking, causing delivery failures for long messages
items.body:
### Bug Description

The standalone platform senders in `tools/send_message_tool.py` (used by both the `send_message` tool and cron job auto-delivery) do not apply message chunking before sending. The gateway adapters handle this correctly since they run messages through `truncate_message()` (defined in `base.py`), which splits at smart boundaries, preserves code blocks across chunks, and adds part indicators. The standalone senders bypass all of that.

Long agent responses delivered via cron jobs or the `send_message` tool fail when they exceed platform length limits. The API rejects the oversized payload. Errors are logged server-side but no message arrives in the chat, so from the user's perspective the delivery fails silently.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a cron job with `deliver: origin` that produces a response longer than the platform's message limit (e.g. >4096 chars for Telegram)
2. Wait for the job to run
3. The response is saved to disk but delivery fails. No message arrives in the chat

Alternatively: have the agent use `send_message` with a message body exceeding the platform limit.

### Expected Behavior

Long messages should be chunked to fit within platform limits before sending, consistent with how the gateway adapters handle regular responses.

### Actual Behavior

The full message is sent as a single API call. Platforms reject it and the user receives nothing.    
Errors are returned in the result dict and logged, but don't surface to the chat. Specifically:

| Platform | Limit | Gateway adapter | `send_message_tool.py` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Telegram | 4,096 chars |chunking via `truncate_message()` | No chunking, single API call |
| Discord | 2,000 chars | chunking via `truncate_message()` | Naive `message[i:i+2000]` split, breaks mid-word/code-block, no part indicators |
| Slack | ~39,000 chars | chunking via `truncate_message()` | No chunking, single API call |
| Signal | ~8,000 chars | No chunking (delegates to daemon) | No chunking, single RPC call |


### Affected Component

Tools (terminal, file ops, web, code execution, etc.)

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

_No response_

### Operating System

Alpine 3.23.3

### Python Version

3.11.14

### Hermes Version

Hermes Agent v0.2.0 (2026.3.12)

### Relevant Logs / Traceback

```shell
ERROR cron.scheduler: Job 'job["id"]': delivery error: Telegram send failed: Message is too long
```

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

The gateway adapters (`gateway/platforms/telegram.py`, `discord.py`, `slack.py`) each call `self.truncate_message()` (defined in `base.py:1080-1168`) in their `send()` method before dispatching to the platform API. This method splits at natural boundaries (newlines, then spaces), preserves code block fences across chunks, and adds `(1/N)` indicators.

The standalone senders in `tools/send_message_tool.py` (`_send_telegram`, `_send_discord`, `_send_slack`, `_send_signal`) call the platform APIs directly without any of that chunking.   
Discord has a naive `[message[i:i+2000]]` split that avoids API rejection but breaks content mid-word and mid-code-block.

Cron delivery in `cron/scheduler.py:_deliver_result()` calls `_send_to_platform()` from `send_message_tool.py`, so it inherits the same gap.

### Proposed Fix (optional)

`truncate_message()` is an instance method on `BasePlatformAdapter` but uses no instance state. Converting it to a `@staticmethod` (following the existing `extract_media()` pattern on the same class) would allow calling it directly as `BasePlatformAdapter.truncate_message(content, max_length)`. `BasePlatformAdapter` is already imported in `send_message_tool.py`.

The chunking can then be applied centrally in `_send_to_platform()` before dispatching to individual senders, using per-platform max lengths. For multi-chunk sends, each chunk is dispatched individually. Media files (Telegram only) attach to the last chunk. Discord's character split in `_send_discord()` would be replaced by the centralized truncate_message() call in ` _send_to_platform()`.

### Problem or Use Case

I want to use api.kilo.ai/api/gateway 

### Proposed Solution

Kilo (kilo.ai) is an AI coding platform whose gateway API is OpenAI-compatible. It'd be great to have it as a built-in provider so users can select it from the provider list and have models auto-populate — same experience as anthropic, openai, etc.

## Description
In the current Gateway logic, MEDIA: and [[audio_as_voice]] tags injected by tool handlers (like TTS) are leaking into the final message output instead of being stripped. This causes these technical directives to appear as raw, unformatted text in the Telegram chat bubble.

## Environment
- Platform: Telegram
- Context: Gateway message handling pipeline
- Tags detected in output: [[audio_as_voice]] and MEDIA:/path/to/audio.ogg

## Expected Behavior
The Gateway (or platform adapter) should intercept and remove these tags from the message body text while using them to trigger the appropriate internal send_voice() logic.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Execute a command that results in a file output (e.g., TTS generation).
2. The Gateway logic injects the media directives into final_response.
3. The platform-specific send() method receives these tags as part of the body text.
4. The tags are rendered as plaintext in the chat client.

## Proposed Solution
Enforce strict tag-stripping within the BasePlatformAdapter's send() or format_message() methods to ensure any injected directives are cleaned before the message text is forwarded to the API.

items.title: search_context() / peer-card retrieval can appear empty immediately after successful session writes while dialectic recall already works
items.body:
Summary
In a self-hosted Honcho deployment, we observed that:
- session writes succeed
- direct session context retrieval succeeds
- dialectic queries can correctly answer about newly written information

…but:
- peer card retrieval may remain empty
- semantic-search-style context retrieval may be sparse or empty immediately after writes

Observed behavior
Using Hermes’ Honcho integration:
- messages are written successfully
- `dialectic_query()` can correctly recall newly written phrases
- `get_peer_card()` often returns `[]`
- `search_context()` is much more useful after explicit conclusions exist than after fresh raw messages alone

Why this is confusing
From an integrator perspective, it can look like:
- “memory works” via dialectic
but
- “search/profile doesn’t work”

Potential interpretations
We’re not yet sure which is intended:
1. peer-card generation is expected to lag and is working as designed
2. search/profile retrieval over raw recent messages is weaker than expected
3. integration assumptions are wrong about when `peer_card` / `peer_representation` should be available

What we tested
- direct writes to session
- direct session context reads
- dialectic Q&A over fresh writes
- search/card retrieval over the same session
- explicit conclusion writes

Interesting result
After writing an explicit conclusion, representation-based search became more useful.
That suggests the issue may be specifically about:
- raw-message-to-representation timing
- or peer-card generation thresholds/selectivity

Question
What should an integrator expect here?
- Is an empty `peer_card` immediately after writes expected?
- Is `search_context` over peer representation intended to exclude recent raw-message content unless it has been derived into observations/card state?

Why this matters
Integrators may want to know whether they should:
- rely on dialectic for continuity
- wait before using search/profile
- or implement a fallback to raw session excerpts when representation/card are empty

items.title: [Feature]: Mitigate plaintext secret (.env) exfiltration risk by adopting Varlock

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

items.body:
### Problem or Use Case

.env files are antiquated! Alarm bells went off for me when I saw my SUDO_PASSWORD stored as plain text in ~/.hermes/.env. Agents are sensitive to prompt injection attacks which could lead to exfiltration of sensitive data. I propose adopting a modern secrets management solution like https://varlock.dev/ (https://github.com/dmno-dev/varlock), which could add a "secure mode" to hermes-agent for users who prefer to manage their secrets via a more robust secret manager tool rather than plain text.

Below is a quick feasibility report. I lean towards Option C listed below, secret manager native, "secure launch" mode.

Happy to draft a PR if support is there.


### Proposed Solution

  Yes — Varlock looks relevant, but only for part of the problem.

   My conclusion

   Varlock appears applicable to Hermes as:
   1. a schema/validation layer for env/config
   2. a safer launcher (`varlock run -- hermes ...`)
   3. a path toward secret-manager-backed config

   But it does not, by itself, eliminate the core risk if Hermes still keeps real secrets
   in `~/.hermes/.env` in plaintext.

   What I found

   About Varlock
   - It is Node-based, but provides a CLI and standalone binary workflow.
   - Core features from its README:
     - `.env.schema` as the source of truth
     - `varlock run -- ...` to inject resolved env into another process
     - leak scanning via `varlock scan`
     - runtime log redaction / leak prevention
     - plugins for secret managers:
       - 1Password
       - AWS Secrets Manager
       - Azure Key Vault
       - GCP Secret Manager
       - Bitwarden
       - Infisical
   - It is explicitly positioned as “AI-safe config”: agents read schema, not secret
   values.

   How Hermes currently works
   Hermes today directly loads plaintext env from `~/.hermes/.env` in several places, e.g.:
   - `run_agent.py`
   - `hermes_cli/main.py`
   - `acp_adapter/entry.py`
   - `cron/scheduler.py`

   That means:
   - secrets are present at rest in a local plaintext file
   - many entrypoints call `load_dotenv(...)` directly
   - if an attacker successfully induces the agent to read or print `.env`, the plaintext
   exists to be exfiltrated

   Hermes does already have some mitigation layers:
   - secret redaction in file/tool outputs
   - some exfiltration pattern detection
   - Tirith command scanning
   - MCP env filtering in some paths

   But those are compensating controls, not a real fix for “plaintext secrets sitting in
   `.env`”.

   So: is Varlock useful?

   Yes, conditionally.

   A. Strong applicability: schema + launcher + secret manager
   Best case:
   - Hermes gets a `.env.schema`
   - real secrets are not stored in `~/.hermes/.env`
   - instead, secrets resolve from a manager via Varlock plugins
   - Hermes is launched via:
     - `varlock run -- hermes ...`
     or
     - `varlock run -- python -m hermes_cli.main ...`

   In that model:
   - the repo gets machine-readable config contracts
   - the agent can be given schema context without values
   - secret values are injected only at runtime
   - plaintext-at-rest risk drops a lot

   This is the most compelling use.

   B. Medium applicability: schema + validation only
   If you keep using plaintext `.env` but add Varlock only for schema/validation:
   - better DX
   - better documentation
   - safer onboarding
   - some leak scanning

   But:
   - the at-rest plaintext secret problem remains

   Useful, but not sufficient.

   C. Weak applicability: direct drop-in replacement
   Varlock is not a trivial drop-in for Hermes today because Hermes is Python and currently
   assumes direct `dotenv` loading in multiple entrypoints.
   You would need some integration work.

   Main integration challenge

   Hermes is not a Node app, but that is not a blocker.
   Varlock’s CLI model is actually a good fit:
   - Hermes does not need to import Varlock as a Python library
   - Hermes can be run under Varlock as a subprocess

   Example pattern:
   - `varlock run -- hermes`
   - `varlock run -- hermes gateway start`
   - `varlock run -- hermes acp`

   That means the easiest integration is operational, not in-process.

   The bigger architectural question is:
   - do you want Hermes to continue loading `~/.hermes/.env` itself?
   - or do you want Hermes to treat external env injection as authoritative?

   Right now Hermes does this:
   - “load ~/.hermes/.env first”
   That behavior would partially undermine Varlock if plaintext `.env` remains the default
   path.

   So the real product decision is not “can we call Varlock?”
   It is:
   - should Hermes support a no-plaintext-secret mode where `.env.schema` exists but secret
   values come from runtime injection / secret managers only?

   Where Varlock fits well

   1. Config contract layer
   Very good fit.
   Hermes would benefit from:
   - explicit env schema
   - sensitivity metadata
   - descriptions / validation
   - a machine-readable contract agents can inspect safely

   This aligns well with your preference for structure over prose.

   2. Launch-time injection
   Also a good fit.
   Hermes could document:
   - preferred secure startup:
     - `varlock run -- hermes`
   - rather than:
     - `hermes` with plaintext `~/.hermes/.env`

   3. Leak scanning
   Potentially useful as an extra defense:
   - pre-commit
   - CI
   - scans for accidental secret leakage

   4. Multi-environment support
   Potentially useful for:
   - local/dev/prod gateway configs
   - different provider stacks
   - ACP/gateway/dev sessions

   Where Varlock does not fully solve the risk

   1. Prompt injection against a live process
   If Hermes has a secret in its environment at runtime, then a sufficiently successful
   compromise may still coerce some code path into revealing it.
   Varlock helps reduce exposure surface, but does not magically prevent runtime access.

   2. Plaintext `~/.hermes/.env` if you keep it
   If the file remains the canonical storage location, the main risk remains.

   3. Python-native integration
   There is no obvious Python-native Varlock library path here; the cleanest route is
   CLI/process integration.

   My recommendation: three pathways

   A. Minimal hardening, low effort
   Keep current model, but reduce obvious risk.
   - continue using `~/.hermes/.env`
   - strengthen redaction and deny-reading of `.env`/credential files
   - add stronger tool-level secret file access restrictions
   - add docs warning against nested repo/plaintext risks
   - maybe add optional encrypted-at-rest `.env` via another mechanism

   Pros:
   - easiest
   Cons:
   - plaintext-at-rest risk remains

   B. Best pragmatic path: Varlock-powered secure mode
   Add first-class support for:
   - `.env.schema`
   - `varlock run -- hermes ...`
   - docs + install path for secure operation
   - optional CI/pre-commit scanning
   - Hermes “doctor” check that detects secure mode / insecure plaintext mode

   In this path:
   - Hermes remains Python
   - Varlock is an external CLI dependency
   - secure users can stop relying on plaintext `.env`

   Pros:
   - real improvement
   - moderate implementation cost
   - no need to rewrite Hermes config system
   Cons:
   - requires Node/binary dependency
   - some entrypoint cleanup needed

   C. Strongest long-term architecture: secret manager native mode
   Hermes should evolve toward:
   - non-secret config in `config.yaml`
   - secrets sourced from OS keyring / 1Password / AWS / Infisical / etc.
   - no plaintext `.env` required
   - optional schema file for AI-safe inspection

   Varlock could still be used here as:
   - schema / tooling / launcher layer
   But Hermes would own the abstraction natively.

   Pros:
   - best security architecture
   Cons:
   - most engineering work

   My recommendation

   I would recommend B first, with C as the long-term direction.

   Concretely:
   1. Introduce `.env.schema` or equivalent secure config contract
   2. Add documented support for launching Hermes under Varlock
   3. Add a “secure mode” where Hermes skips direct `~/.hermes/.env` loading if a flag is
   set, and expects env injection from the parent process
   4. Encourage secret-manager plugins instead of plaintext local secrets
   5. Tighten tool-level protections against reading `.env` directly

   Why this is the right middle ground
   - it materially reduces risk
   - it does not require rewriting Hermes around Node
   - it matches Hermes’ multi-entrypoint architecture
   - it preserves backward compatibility

   What I would change in Hermes specifically

   If implemented well, I’d suggest:

   1. New secure-launch mode
   Something like:
   - `HERMES_ENV_SOURCE=external`
   or
   - `HERMES_DISABLE_DOTENV=1`

   Behavior:
   - do not load `~/.hermes/.env`
   - trust inherited process env only

   Then users can do:
   - `varlock run -- hermes`
   - `varlock run -- hermes gateway start`

   2. Add `.env.schema`
   Not for secrets themselves, but for:
   - variable names
   - types
   - descriptions
   - sensitivity labels
   - defaults for non-secret values

   3. Doctor warning
   `hermes doctor` should warn if:
   - sensitive vars are stored in plaintext `~/.hermes/.env`
   - secure mode is not enabled

   4. Stronger secret-file protections
   Hermes should consider stricter blocking around:
   - reading `.env`
   - `.netrc`
   - auth.json
   - cloud credential files

   5. Secret source abstraction later
   Long-term, formalize:
   - env
   - keyring
   - secret manager
   as first-class secret backends

   Bottom line

   Varlock is applicable to Hermes, but mainly as:
   - a schema and secure launcher
   - not as a magic fix

   If Hermes keeps using plaintext `~/.hermes/.env` as the default canonical secret store,
   the core problem remains.
   If Hermes adopts a secure external-env mode and uses Varlock + secret-manager plugins,
   then yes — this could be a meaningful mitigation.

### Alternatives Considered

_No response_

### Feature Type

New tool

items.title: Add support for multiple providers or base_url config in compression
items.body:
**Issue Type:** Feature Request

**Current Behavior:**
When using a custom provider (like zai) for the compression model, there's no way to specify a custom base URL. The compression model currently only accepts a `summary_model` name, not a full provider configuration.

**Problem Example:**
```yaml
compression:
  enabled: true
  threshold: 0.85
  summary_model: google/gemini-3-flash-preview  # Uses default provider
  summary_provider: auto
```

But if you want to use a custom provider like zai:
```yaml
compression:
  enabled: true
  threshold: 0.85
  summary_model: glm-4.7
  summary_provider: zai
```

This fails if zai doesn't support Google models, and there's no way to specify a custom base_url for the compression model.

**Requested Solution:**
Either:

1. **Option A:** Allow compression model to accept a full provider config (similar to `smart_model_routing`):
```yaml
compression:
  enabled: true
  threshold: 0.85
  summary_model:
    provider: zai
    model: glm-4.7
    base_url: https://api.z.ai/api/coding/paas/v4
```

2. **Option B:** Allow compression model to accept a `base_url` parameter:
```yaml
compression:
  enabled: true
  threshold: 0.85
  summary_model: glm-4.7
  summary_provider: zai
  summary_base_url: https://api.z.ai/api/coding/paas/v4
```

**Use Case:**
Multiple providers exist (zai, DeepSeek, OpenRouter, etc.) with different models and API endpoints. Users should be able to configure custom providers for the compression model without modifying the core code.

**Suggested Implementation:**
- Update the compression config schema to accept either a full model config or a base_url parameter
- Follow the existing pattern used in `smart_model_routing`

items.title: feat(gateway): inject reply-to message context when quoted message is not in session history
items.body:
## Problem

When a user replies to a specific message on Telegram (or other platforms), the agent has no visibility into which message is being referenced. The `MessageEvent` dataclass has a `reply_to_message_id` field, but:

1. The Telegram adapter's `_build_message_event()` never populates it
2. There is no field for the replied-to message's text content
3. The gateway never injects the quoted text into the agent's context

This is especially problematic when replying to messages that are **outside the current session context** — cron job results, `/background` task outputs, messages from previous sessions, or messages that were compressed away. The agent receives the user's reply with zero context about what it refers to.

## Proposed Solution

A token-efficient approach that only adds context when needed:

1. **`MessageEvent`** — add `reply_to_text: Optional[str]` field
2. **Telegram adapter** — populate `reply_to_message_id` and `reply_to_text` from `message.reply_to_message` (Telegram already sends the full quoted message in the update — no extra API call needed)
3. **Gateway message handler** — before running the agent, check if the replied-to text appears in the conversation history:
   - **Found in history** → do nothing (zero extra tokens)
   - **Not found** → prepend `[Replying to: "<quoted text>"]` to the message

This keeps token usage minimal for normal same-session replies while providing critical context for cross-session/cron/background replies.

## Use Cases Solved

- Replying to **cron job results** (delivered via `adapter.send()`, not in session transcript)
- Replying to **`/background` task outputs**
- Replying to **messages from previous sessions** (after `/new` or context compression)
- Replying to **old messages** that were compressed away
- Future: replying to **background delegation results**

## Files Changed

items.title: feat(delegation): add background=true mode for fire-and-forget subagent tasks

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

items.body:
## Problem

`delegate_task()` always blocks the parent agent until the subagent completes. For long-running tasks (web research, browser automation, complex analysis), this blocks the entire conversation — the user can't interact with the agent while the subagent runs.

The `/background` slash command already provides fire-and-forget execution at the gateway level, but there's no way for the agent to **programmatically** choose to run a delegation in the background.

## Proposed Solution

Add a `background` parameter to `delegate_task()`. When `background=true`:

1. The child agent spawns in a daemon thread
2. `delegate_task()` returns immediately with `{"status": "dispatched", "background_task_id": "..."}`
3. The parent agent can respond to the user and continue the conversation
4. When the child finishes, the gateway delivers the result to the user's chat — same delivery flow as `/background`

## Use Cases

- **Long-running research tasks**: agent fires off a web research subagent and keeps chatting
- **Browser automation**: delegating tasks that take 60+ seconds (e.g., Oracle CLI browser mode)
- **Parallel workflows**: fire multiple background delegations while maintaining conversation flow
- **Any task where blocking the conversation is worse than async delivery**

## Design

Follows the same pattern as `/background` and process watchers:

- New `tools/background_delegation_registry.py` — simple registry tracking background threads (parallel to `process_registry`)
- `delegate_task()` gains `background` param — when true, spawns thread, registers in registry, returns immediately
- Gateway picks up pending background delegations (same spot as process watchers) and creates async watcher tasks
- Watcher polls for completion, delivers result via `adapter.send()`

## Constraints

- `background=true` only works for single tasks, not batch mode
- Results are always delivered as standalone messages (not injected into session context)
- Single-task only (batch + background doesn't make sense — batch already runs children in parallel and waits)

---

items.title: Bug: Claude Code OAuth endpoint returns generic 400 treated as non-retryable
items.body:
# Bug: Claude Code OAuth endpoint returns generic 400 treated as non-retryable

## Summary

When using Anthropic's Claude Code OAuth authentication (`ANTHROPIC_TOKEN` / Bearer auth), the API intermittently returns `400 Bad Request` with a generic error body (`"message": "Error"`). Hermes classifies all 400s as non-retryable client errors and aborts immediately, but these responses are actually transient server-side failures — the same request succeeds on a subsequent attempt.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.2.0 (commit `57be18c`)
- Auth: Claude Code OAuth (`sk-ant-oat01-*` token via `ANTHROPIC_TOKEN`)
- OS: WSL2 (Ubuntu) on Windows 11
- Python 3.11.15

## Behavior

The Claude Code OAuth endpoint (`oauth-2025-04-20` + `claude-code-20250219` betas) is less stable than the direct API. It intermittently returns two types of transient errors:

1. **500 Internal Server Error** — already handled by the retry loop, recovers on attempt 2-3
2. **400 Bad Request** with `{"type": "invalid_request_error", "message": "Error"}` — treated as non-retryable, causes immediate abort

Both errors are transient and originate server-side. The key evidence: the same request payload (same model, same tools, same messages) succeeds on retry. A genuine invalid request would fail 100% of the time and return a specific error message (e.g., "invalid model", "unknown parameter").

The generic 400 is distinguishable from a real client error by its message field: real `invalid_request_error` responses include a descriptive message, while the transient ones contain just `"Error"` or an empty string.

## Reproduction

1. Configure Hermes with Claude Code OAuth auth (`ANTHROPIC_TOKEN=sk-ant-oat01-*`)
2. Start a session: `hermes chat --yolo -q "What time is it?"`
3. Repeat ~5-10 times — some requests will fail with 400 on the first attempt

The failure rate varies but is roughly 1 in 3 requests. Sessions with tool use (45 tools loaded) seem more affected than simple text-only exchanges, though both can trigger it.

## Request dump from a failed attempt

```json
{
  "model": "claude-opus-4-6",
  "tools": 45,
  "thinking": {"type": "adaptive"},
  "messages": 5,
  "reason": "non_retryable_client_error",
  "error": {
    "type": "error",
    "error": {
      "type": "invalid_request_error",
      "message": "Error"
    },
    "request_id": "req_011CZ7iZhtNkAygHh1aymXrY"
  }
}
```

Note the empty `"message": "Error"` — no indication of what's actually invalid.

## Suggested fix

In `run_agent.py`, the `is_client_status_error` check treats all `400 <= status < 500` (except 413) as non-retryable. Add an exception for generic 400s where the error message is just `"Error"` or empty:

```python
# Exception: the Claude Code OAuth endpoint sometimes returns
# 400 with a bare "Error" message on transient server failures.
# These are retryable — a real invalid_request_error has a
# specific message (e.g. "invalid model", "unknown parameter").
_err_body = getattr(api_error, "body", None) or {}
_err_message = (_err_body.get("error", {}).get("message", "") if isinstance(_err_body, dict) else "")
_is_generic_400 = status_code == 400 and _err_message.strip().lower() in ("error", "")
is_local_validation_error = isinstance(api_error, (ValueError, TypeError))
is_client_status_error = isinstance(status_code, int) and 400 <= status_code < 500 and status_code != 413 and not _is_generic_400
```

This lets generic 400s fall through to the existing retry loop (with exponential backoff), while preserving immediate abort for real client errors like 401, 403, 404, 422, and 400s with specific error messages.

## Impact

Without this fix, Claude Code OAuth users experience frequent session failures that require manual retry. With the fix applied locally, sessions recover transparently — the generic 400 retries and succeeds on the next attempt, same as the existing 500 handling.

items.title: [Bug]: gateway should recover unloaded launchd jobs and report stale service state
items.body:
## Summary

There are still a few residual service-management bugs in `hermes gateway` after #1567.

They all show up when a local service definition exists but the service manager state is stale or broken:

1. `install` only checks whether the plist/unit file exists, so a stale service definition is skipped instead of repaired.
2. `launchd start` does not recover from `launchctl start ai.hermes.gateway` returning exit status `3` when the job is unloaded.
3. `gateway restart` swallows launchd/systemd restart failures and falls back to foreground `run_gateway()`, which can make the service look recovered when the background service is still broken.
4. `launchd status` only reports whether the job is loaded; it does not surface that a local plist exists and is stale/out-of-sync with the current install.

## Environment

- OS: macOS 15.6 / Darwin 24.6.0 x86_64
- Python: 3.11.14
- Hermes: `Hermes Agent v0.2.0 (2026.3.12)`
- Repo state: `main` at `cfa87e77`

## Reproduction

### 1. Stale service definition is skipped by install

1. Install the gateway service.
2. Move or rename the repo, or otherwise make the generated `WorkingDirectory` / `ProgramArguments` differ from the installed plist.
3. Run `hermes gateway install` again without `--force`.

Observed:
- The command exits with "Service already installed" and leaves the stale plist/unit untouched.

Expected:
- If the local service definition exists but no longer matches the current install, `install` should repair it automatically.

### 2. `launchd start` cannot self-heal an unloaded job

1. Have `~/Library/LaunchAgents/ai.hermes.gateway.plist` present.
2. Ensure the launchd job is not loaded (for example, `launchctl unload ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ai.hermes.gateway.plist`).
3. Run `hermes gateway start`.

Observed:
- `launchctl start ai.hermes.gateway` returns exit status `3` and the CLI does not retry with `launchctl load`.

Expected:
- If the plist exists locally and `start` fails because the job is unloaded, Hermes should load the plist and retry once.

### 3. `gateway restart` masks broken service state

1. Have a gateway plist/unit file present.
2. Put the service manager into a broken/unloaded state so service restart fails.
3. Run `hermes gateway restart`.

Observed:
- The restart failure is swallowed.
- Hermes falls back to `run_gateway(verbose=False)` in the foreground.
- This makes the gateway appear recovered, while the managed background service is still broken.

Expected:
- If a service definition exists but service restart fails, the command should report that failure clearly and exit non-zero instead of silently switching to a foreground process.

### 4. `launchd status` lacks local/stale plist diagnostics

1. Leave a stale or outdated `~/Library/LaunchAgents/ai.hermes.gateway.plist` on disk.
2. Ensure the job is not loaded.
3. Run `hermes gateway status`.

Observed:
- Output only says the service is not loaded.
- It does not mention the local plist path, whether the plist is stale, or that a repair/start command would reload it.

Expected:
- `status` should show the local plist path and whether it matches the current generated service definition, so the user can distinguish "not installed" from "installed but stale/unloaded".

## Why this matters

These are all bug-fix / robustness issues in the service-management path:

- They affect macOS specifically, which is one of Hermes' supported platforms.
- They make service recovery brittle after repo moves or failed loads.
- They hide true background service failures behind a foreground fallback.
- They make diagnosis harder than it needs to be.

I have a patch ready that adds targeted recovery + tests for these cases and will open a PR linked to this issue.

## Bug

When the primary model hits a rate limit and the agent falls back to a backup model (e.g., `minimax/minimax-m2.5` via OpenRouter), the `/model` command still displays the primary model from `config.yaml` (e.g., `gpt-5.4`). The agent itself also reports the wrong model when asked.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure a primary model (`gpt-5.4` via `openai-codex`) with a fallback (`minimax/minimax-m2.5` via `openrouter`)
2. Send messages until the primary model's rate limit is hit
3. Observe `Fallback activated: gpt-5.4 → minimax/minimax-m2.5 (openrouter)` in logs
4. Send `/model` in Telegram
5. Response shows `Current model: gpt-5.4 / Provider: OpenAI Codex` — wrong

## Root Cause

`_handle_model_command` in `gateway/run.py` reads the model from `config.yaml` and env vars:

```python
current = os.getenv("HERMES_MODEL") or "gpt-5.4"
# ... then reads config.yaml model.default
```

But `_try_activate_fallback` in `run_agent.py` only updates the `AIAgent` instance's runtime state (`self.model`, `self.provider`), which is discarded after the agent run completes. The gateway has no persistent record that a fallback is active.

## Expected Behavior

`/model` should show the **actually active** model and indicate when running on a fallback:

```
🤖 Current model: minimax/minimax-m2.5 (fallback)
Provider: OpenRouter
Primary model (gpt-5.4 via OpenAI Codex) is rate-limited.
```

## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.2.x (latest main)
- Gateway mode with Telegram
- Primary: `gpt-5.4` via `openai-codex`
- Fallback: `minimax/minimax-m2.5` via `openrouter`

items.title: Gateway systemd service fails to auto-restart when browser processes orphaned
items.body:
## Problem

When the gateway spawns browser automation (Chrome via `remote-debugging-port`), those Chrome child processes join the systemd service cgroup. On service stop/restart:

1. `ExecStop` triggers graceful Python shutdown
2. Python's async Telegram disconnect throws errors (`'NoneType' object has no attribute 'shutdown'`, `dictionary changed size during iteration`)
3. systemd waits `TimeoutStopSec` (15s), then tries to kill the cgroup
4. Chrome orphans prevent clean cgroup teardown: `Failed to kill control group: Invalid argument`
5. Service enters `Failed with result 'timeout'` state
6. `Restart=on-failure` doesn't always trigger recovery after this state

The gateway stays down until manually restarted.

## Root Causes

- **`KillMode=mixed`** only SIGKILLs the main process, leaving chrome children alive in the cgroup
- **`Restart=on-failure`** doesn't cover all exit scenarios (e.g., SIGKILL after timeout)
- **No cleanup** of leaked browser processes after stop
- **No crash loop protection** — if something is broken, it could restart infinitely

## Fix

Update `generate_systemd_unit()` in `hermes_cli/gateway.py`:

- `Restart=always` — self-heal on any exit
- `KillMode=control-group` — kill entire cgroup including orphan chromes
- `ExecStopPost` — force-kill leaked browser processes
- `StartLimitIntervalSec=120` / `StartLimitBurst=5` — crash loop protection
- `TimeoutStopSec=20` — slightly more time for graceful disconnect
- `SendSIGKILL=yes` — ensure cleanup after timeout
- `RestartSec=15` — prevent rapid restart churn

Users who already installed the service need to run `hermes gateway install --force` to regenerate the unit file.

### Bug Description

`hermes --version` reports "Update available: 26 commits behind — run 'hermes update'" even though the local
   repo is already at the latest commit on `origin/main`

### Steps to Reproduce

  **Scenario A (manual git pull + hermes update):**
   1. Run `git pull` in the hermes-agent directory — pulls latest commits
   2. Run `hermes update` — correctly says "✓ Already up to date!"
   3. Run `hermes --version` — still shows "Update available: 26 commits behind"

   **Scenario B (stale cache persists after hermes update):**
   1. Have a stale `.update_check` cache (written before new commits were available)
   2. Run `hermes update` — fetches and pulls new commits successfully
   3. Run `hermes --version` — still shows stale "commits behind" count from cache

### Expected Behavior

No update banner when local HEAD == origin/main HEAD

### Actual Behavior

False positive "26 commits behind" message

### Affected Component

CLI (interactive chat), Gateway (Telegram/Discord/Slack/WhatsApp)

### Operating System

Linux aarch64 (Raspberry Pi, Debian)

### Python Version

3.11.15

### Hermes Version

v0.2.0 (2026.3.12)


### Root Cause Analysis (optional)
   The update checker in `hermes_cli/banner.py` caches results to `~/.hermes/.update_check`
   for 6 hours (`_UPDATE_CHECK_CACHE_SECONDS = 6 * 3600`). When `hermes --version` runs,
   it reads this cache and returns the stale `behind` count without re-running `git rev-list`.

   The problem: `cmd_update()` in `hermes_cli/main.py` never invalidates this cache file
   after a successful update. Two code paths are affected:

   1. **Full pull path** — `hermes update` fetches and pulls new commits, but `.update_check`
      still contains the old `behind` count
   2. **"Already up to date" path** — user runs `git pull` manually first, then `hermes update`
      says "Already up to date!" and returns early — but the stale cache from before the
      manual pull is never cleared

   Cache file location: `~/.hermes/.update_check`
   Cache read: `banner.py` line 159 — returns cached value if less than 6h old
   Missing invalidation: `main.py` `cmd_update()` — neither the early return (line 2199)

items.title: [Bug]: Gateway enters infinite 400 failure loop when Telegram session exceeds context limits
items.body:
### Bug Description

   When a Telegram conversation session grows large enough to exceed Anthropic's API context limits, the
   gateway enters an infinite failure loop. Every subsequent message from the user fails with a 400
   `invalid_request_error`, and the session never auto-recovers because:

   1. Anthropic returns `"message": "Error"` (no descriptive text) — the agent's compression recovery only
   checks for phrases like "context length", "token limit", "prompt is too long" (`run_agent.py:5477-5483`),
   none of which match
   2. The gateway has no 400-specific error handling — it shows a generic error and suggests `/reset`
   (`gateway/run.py:1997-2014`)
   3. The failed user message still gets persisted to the session, making it even larger
   4. Next message → same failure. Loop repeats indefinitely.

   Observed it live myself: a TG session grew to 347 messages / 621KB, producing 17 consecutive 400 errors over
   several hours.

### Steps to Reproduce

   1. Start a Telegram conversation via the gateway
   2. Have an extended conversation with many tool calls (large tool outputs accelerate this)
   3. Don't use `/new` or `/reset` — let the session grow naturally over 1-2 days
   4. Eventually the API call exceeds context limits
   5. Every subsequent message now fails with: `Error code: 400 - {'type': 'error', 'error': {'type':
   'invalid_request_error', 'message': 'Error'}}`
   6. The only recovery is the user manually typing `/reset` — but the error message doesn't clearly tell them
   to do so

### Expected Behavior

   When a 400 error occurs due to oversized context, the gateway should:
   - Detect the oversized session and auto-compress or auto-reset
   - At minimum, not persist the failed user message (which makes the session even larger)
   - Give the user a clear message like "Session too large, auto-compressing..." instead of a generic error

### Actual Behavior

   - Generic error message shown to user
   - Failed messages still persisted to session (session grows on each failure)
   - No auto-compression triggered (error message "Error" doesn't match any recovery phrases)
   - Infinite failure loop until user manually runs `/reset`

### Affected Component

Gateway (Telegram/Discord/Slack/WhatsApp), Agent Core (conversation loop, context compression, memory)

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

Telegram

### Operating System

Debian (aarch64, Raspberry Pi)

### Python Version

3.11.15

### Hermes Version

v0.2.0 (build 2026.3.12)

### Relevant Logs / Traceback

```shell
2026-03-17 11:12:15,579 INFO anthropic._base_client: Retrying request to /v1/messages in 0.390310 seconds
   2026-03-17 11:12:15,979 INFO anthropic._base_client: Retrying request to /v1/messages in 0.896718 seconds
   2026-03-17 11:12:18,158 ERROR root: Non-retryable client error: Error code: 400 - {'type': 'error', 'error':
   {'type': 'invalid_request_error', 'message': 'Error'}, 'request_id': 'req_011CZ87pjDLeyMUfLMeKm5YE'}
   

   Request dump shows: 347 messages, 621KB request body, model `claude-opus-4-6`.
```

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

Multiple contributing factors:
   | # | Issue | Location | Severity |
   |---|-------|----------|----------|
   | 1 | Anthropic returns `"message": "Error"` — no keyword match triggers compression | `run_agent.py:5477-5483` | Critical |
   | 2 | No 400-specific error handling in gateway | `gateway/run.py:1997-2014` | High |
   | 3 | Rough token estimate threshold inflated to 119% of context via 1.4x safety factor |`gateway/run.py:1594-1596` | Medium |
   | 4 | Failed user messages still persisted to session — session grows during failure loop |`run_agent.py:5577`, `gateway/run.py:1946-1975` | High |

   The phrase matching at `run_agent.py:5477-5483`:
   ```python
   is_context_length_error = any(phrase in error_msg for phrase in [
       'context length', 'context size', 'maximum context',
       'token limit', 'too many tokens', 'reduce the length',
       'exceeds the limit', 'context window',
       'request entity too large', 'prompt is too long',
   ])
   ```
   None match `"Error"`.

### Proposed Fix (optional)

   1. Add 400 recovery in `gateway/run.py`: when `status_code == 400` and session is large (>100 messages or
   >200KB), auto-compress before retrying
   2. Add catch-all: treat ANY 400 `invalid_request_error` from Anthropic as a potential context-length error
   when session is above 50% of model context
   3. Don't persist failed user messages when the agent returns `{"failed": True}` before generating any
   response
   4. Add a circuit breaker: after 3 consecutive 400 failures on the same session, force-compress or
   force-reset

 After restarting the gateway (e.g. `hermes gateway run --replace`), `gateway_state.json` still shows the old
   process's PID instead of the new one. The `gateway.pid` file is correct — only `gateway_state.json` is
   stale.

### Steps to Reproduce

   1. Start the gateway: `hermes gateway run`
   2. Note the PID (e.g. 36459)
   3. Restart: `hermes gateway run --replace`
   4. Check actual PID: `ps aux | grep gateway` → shows new PID (e.g. 8820)
   5. Check `~/.hermes/gateway_state.json` → still shows old PID 36459
   6. Check `~/.hermes/gateway.pid` → correctly shows 8820

### Expected Behavior

`gateway_state.json` should show the current gateway process PID (8820) after restart.

`gateway_state.json` retains the old PID (36459). `gateway.pid` is correct.

### Affected Component

Gateway (Telegram/Discord/Slack/WhatsApp)

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

Telegram

### Operating System

Debian (aarch64, Raspberry Pi)

### Python Version

3.11.15

### Hermes Version

v0.2.0 (build 2026.3.12)

```shell

```

Bug is in `gateway/status.py` lines 195-199, in `write_runtime_status()`:

   ```python
   payload = _read_json_file(path) or _build_runtime_status_record()  # reads OLD file
   payload.setdefault("platforms", {})
   payload.setdefault("kind", _GATEWAY_KIND)
   ```

items.title: [Feature] Support multiple configured providers with ordered fallback sequence (like pi-mono)
items.body:
### Problem or Use Case

Currently Hermes Agent only supports configuring one primary provider/model and one single fallback provider/model. When the primary provider hits rate limits, goes down, or returns errors, and the single fallback also fails, the agent can't continue and must stop.

  I want to configure multiple providers/models (with different API keys or different providers) so that if one fails, Hermes can automatically try the next one in sequence and keep working without manual intervention. This is especially useful for:
  - Avoiding interruptions when hitting rate limits
  - Having backup providers if one service is experiencing outages
  - Cost optimization by trying cheaper providers first
  - Reliability for long-running agent tasks

### Proposed Solution

Add support for an ordered fallback list in the configuration. Here's the proposed config structure that maintains backward compatibility:
```
 model:
    provider: "anthropic"
    default: "claude-sonnet-4-6"

  # New: multiple fallbacks in priority order
  # If primary fails, try first fallback, if that fails, try second, etc.
  fallback_models:
    - provider: "openrouter"
      model: "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6"
    - provider: "openrouter"
      model: "anthropic/claude-3.5-sonnet"
    - provider: "custom"
      model: "claude-sonnet-4-6"
```
  Behavior:
  1. When making an LLM API call, start with the primary model.provider / model.default
  2. If the call fails (any error: rate limit, timeout, API error, connectivity issue),
  automatically try the next entry in fallback_models
  3. Continue until either a call succeeds or all configured fallbacks are exhausted
  4. This applies to all model calls (main model, smart_model_routing, auxiliary vision, etc.)
  5. Existing fallback_model config can still be supported for backward compatibility by
  converting it to a single-entry fallback_models list

  Alternative (cleaner approach that replaces the single fallback):
```
  model:
    try_order:
      - provider: "anthropic"
        model: "claude-sonnet-4-6"
      - provider: "openrouter"
        model: "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6"
      - provider: "openrouter"
        model: "anthropic/claude-3.5-sonnet"
```
  This is similar to the pattern used in https://hochej.github.io/pi-mono/coding-agent/models/
  which has proven to work well.

items.title: [Bug]: hermes gateway systemd unit omits nvm Node path and crash-loops with WhatsApp enabled
items.body:
## Bug description
When Hermes is installed on Linux with Node.js available only through `nvm`, `hermes gateway install` writes a systemd user unit whose PATH does not include the resolved Node binary directory. If WhatsApp is enabled, the gateway service enters a restart loop because the WhatsApp bridge requirement check cannot find `node` under the service environment.

## Reproduction
Fresh repro on Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS (WSL2), upstream `main`.

### Environment
- OS: Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS
- Hermes commit: `548cedb8694b198a67a521fb0186dd8dd5a449d3`
- Python: 3.12 system Python, installer created a 3.11 venv
- Node install method: `nvm`
- Node version: `v24.14.0`

### Steps
1. Install Node with `nvm` so `node` is available in an interactive shell but lives under `~/.nvm/.../bin/node`.
2. Install Hermes from upstream `main`.
3. Add the following to `~/.hermes/.env`:
   ```bash
   WHATSAPP_ENABLED=true
   WHATSAPP_MODE=bot
   ```
4. Install the user gateway service:
   ```bash
   hermes gateway install
   ```
5. Restart and inspect the service:
   ```bash
   systemctl --user restart hermes-gateway
   systemctl --user status hermes-gateway --no-pager
   journalctl --user -u hermes-gateway --no-pager -n 80
   ```
6. Inspect the generated unit PATH / run the WhatsApp requirement check under the same environment.

## Expected behavior
The generated systemd user unit should include the directory containing the currently-resolved `node` binary, so the WhatsApp bridge can start successfully when Node is installed via `nvm`.

## Actual behavior
The generated unit contains a PATH like:
```text
/home/<user>/.../venv/bin:/home/<user>/.../node_modules/.bin:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin
```
which omits `~/.nvm/versions/node/.../bin`.

As a result:
- `node` is missing under the service environment
- `check_whatsapp_requirements()` returns `False`
- the gateway exits and systemd restart-loops it if WhatsApp is enabled

## Minimal evidence
Generated unit PATH omitted the resolved Node directory.

Under the same service-like environment:
```text
NODE_MISSING
CHECK_WHATSAPP_REQUIREMENTS False
```

## Why this matters
This is a clean install failure path for WhatsApp on Linux systems where Node is installed through `nvm`, which is a common setup. The interactive shell works, but the background service does not.

## Proposed fix
When generating the systemd unit, include `dirname(shutil.which("node"))` in the service PATH if `node` resolves during `hermes gateway install`.

items.title: [Bug]: send_message advertises WhatsApp but outbound WhatsApp routing is not implemented
items.body:
## Bug description
The `send_message` tool advertises WhatsApp as a supported platform and maps `"whatsapp"` to `Platform.WHATSAPP`, but the actual outbound routing function `_send_to_platform(...)` has no WhatsApp branch. As a result, any outbound WhatsApp send through `send_message` fails immediately with:

```text
Direct sending not yet implemented for whatsapp
```

This breaks proactive WhatsApp delivery paths such as reminders / cron notifications that rely on `send_message`.

## Why this is a real bug
This is not a pairing or connectivity issue. The failure happens before any WhatsApp bridge call is attempted:
- `send_message` accepts `whatsapp` as a target platform
- the local WhatsApp bridge already exposes a `/send` endpoint
- `_send_to_platform(...)` simply never routes WhatsApp to a sender

## Reproduction
Reproduced from upstream `main` at commit:
`548cedb8694b198a67a521fb0186dd8dd5a449d3`

### Minimal code reproduction
From a clean checkout of upstream `main`:

```python
import sys, asyncio
sys.path.insert(0, '/path/to/hermes-agent')
from tools.send_message_tool import _send_to_platform
from gateway.config import Platform
from types import SimpleNamespace

pconfig = SimpleNamespace(token=None, extra={})
result = asyncio.run(_send_to_platform(Platform.WHATSAPP, pconfig, '12345@lid', 'hello'))
print(result)
```

### Actual result
```python
{'error': 'Direct sending not yet implemented for whatsapp'}
```

### Expected result
WhatsApp should be routed through the existing local bridge send path, analogous to how other supported platforms are routed through their respective send helpers.

## Additional evidence
In upstream `tools/send_message_tool.py`:
- `"whatsapp": Platform.WHATSAPP` is present in the platform map
- but `_send_to_platform(...)` has no `Platform.WHATSAPP` branch
- and there is no `_send_whatsapp(...)` helper

## Impact
This prevents outbound WhatsApp messaging through the shared `send_message` tool, which in turn breaks proactive delivery flows that depend on it.

## Proposed fix
Add a WhatsApp sender branch in `_send_to_platform(...)` and implement `_send_whatsapp(...)` using the existing local bridge HTTP `/send` endpoint.

items.title: STT Provider Selection Logic: Placeholder API keys treated as valid credentials
items.body:
## Bug Description

The `_get_provider()` function in `transcription_tools.py` incorrectly treats placeholder/dummy API keys as valid credentials, causing it to select the OpenAI provider instead of falling back to local STT when `provider: local` is configured.

## Root Cause

In `_resolve_openai_api_key()` (line ~218), the function returns any non-empty string as a "valid" API key. This means:
- `disabled-use-local-whisper` (a placeholder value) is treated as valid
- `_get_provider()` at line ~187 checks `if _HAS_OPENAI and _resolve_openai_api_key():` - returns truthy
- Even though the key is invalid, the provider logic selects OpenAI
- This bypasses the intended local STT fallback

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Set `OPENAI_API_KEY=disabled-use-local-whisper` (or any non-empty placeholder) in environment
2. Set `stt: provider: local` in config.yaml  
3. Ensure `faster-whisper` is NOT installed (`_HAS_FASTER_WHISPER = False`)
4. Try to transcribe a voice message
5. Observe 401 error from OpenAI API instead of graceful fallback or error

## Expected Behavior

When `provider: local` is configured, the system should:
1. Attempt to use local STT (faster-whisper) if available
2. If faster-whisper is not available, fail gracefully with a clear error message
3. Never use a placeholder/non-standard API key value as valid credentials

## Actual Behavior

The system sends requests to OpenAI with the placeholder key, resulting in 401 authentication errors.

## Environment

- File: `hermes_agent/tools/transcription_tools.py`
- Key function: `_get_provider()` (lines ~164-236)
- Related: `_resolve_openai_api_key()` (line ~218)

## Proposed Solutions

### Option A: Validate API key format
Check that the key starts with `sk-` (OpenAI standard) before treating it as valid:
```python
def _resolve_openai_api_key():
    key = _config.get("openai_api_key") or os.environ.get("OPENAI_API_KEY")
    if key and key.startswith("sk-"):
        return key
    return None
```

### Option B: Respect explicit config provider setting
When `provider: local` is explicitly set, never fall back to OpenAI regardless of what API keys are present. The current logic only checks `faster_whisper` availability, not the user's explicit preference.

### Option C: Whitelist valid provider configs
Only consider a provider available if both:
1. The library is installed (e.g., `_HAS_OPENAI`)
2. A valid API key format is detected (starts with `sk-`)

## Additional Context

- The `_HAS_FASTER_WHISPER` flag determines if local STT is available
- When False, the code falls through to check cloud providers (Groq, then OpenAI)
- This creates a dependency on OpenAI even when the user explicitly configured local STT
- The logic assumes any non-empty string is a valid API key, which breaks intentional "disable" patterns like `disabled-use-local-whisper`

items.title: Telegram streaming edit fails with Message_too_long instead of falling back/splitting
items.body:
## Summary

When Telegram gateway streaming is enabled, a long streamed reply can fail once the edited message grows past Telegram's 4096-character limit.

The normal send path chunks long messages, but the streaming edit path does not. The result is `telegram.error.BadRequest: Message_too_long`, after which the handler returns empty/None and the response dies.

## Repro

1. Enable Telegram gateway streaming.
2. Send a prompt that produces a long reply while streaming is active.
3. Once the in-place edited message exceeds Telegram's max length, Hermes logs:
   - `Failed to edit Telegram message <id>: Message_too_long`
   - then `Handler returned empty/None response`

## Why this looks like a real bug

The normal Telegram send path formats and splits messages before sending:
- `gateway/platforms/telegram.py` -> `send()`
- `gateway/platforms/base.py` -> `truncate_message()`

But the Telegram streaming edit path just calls `edit_message_text()` on the full accumulated content:
- `gateway/platforms/telegram.py` -> `edit_message()`

So long non-streamed replies are handled, but long streamed replies are not.

## Expected behavior

One of:
- gracefully stop in-place editing before the Telegram limit and send the remainder as follow-up chunks
- or detect overlong edits and fall back to a non-streaming multi-message send
- or otherwise degrade cleanly instead of aborting the reply

## Notes

This is separate from `Message is not modified` and separate from Telegram flood control / `RetryAfter` behavior.

The issue here is specifically the length mismatch between the chunked send path and the unchunked edit path.

items.title: [Feature]: Add Feishu as a supported gateway / messaging platform
items.body:
### Problem or Use Case

Hermes currently supports several messaging platforms in the gateway layer, such as Telegram, Discord, Slack, and WhatsApp, but it does not support Feishu /  Lark.

This makes Hermes harder to adopt in teams and companies that use Feishu as their primary internal messaging platform, especially in China-based workflows. In practice, this means users cannot run Hermes as a bot inside Feishu group chats or direct conversations, even though the gateway architecture already supports similar platform adapters.

### Proposed Solution

Add Feishu as a first-class gateway platform adapter, following the existing platform architecture under `gateway/platforms/`.

The implementation would include:

  - a new `gateway/platforms/feishu.py` adapter
  - gateway config support for Feishu-specific credentials and settings
  - integration in `gateway/run.py`
  - compatibility updates for message sending / reply flows
  - tests for config and platform behavior
  - README documentation for setup and usage

This should behave consistently with the existing messaging platform adapters and reuse the same gateway conventions where possible.

### Alternatives Considered

One alternative is to use Feishu through a generic webhook bridge or external relay service, but that adds operational complexity and loses the consistency of Hermes' native platform integrations.

Another alternative is to keep Feishu support outside the main repo, but this is less discoverable and less maintainable for users who expect messaging platforms to be supported directly in the gateway layer.
